claim_text: OpenAI's models went on to access the production infrastructure of Hugging Face.
quote: The models went on to access the production infrastructure of Hugging Face, a platform for open-source machine learning models and AI datasets.

claim_text: After reviewing 141,006 evaluation runs, Anthropic identified three incidents.
quote: After reviewing 141,006 evaluation runs where Claude could have obtained internet access, we identified three incidents in which a model accessed the internet from within or while interacting with the evaluation environment of Irregular, one of our third-party evaluation partners, and then gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three different organizations.

claim_text: The incidents involved three different Claude models: Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and an internal research test model.
quote: The incidents involved three different Claude models: Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and an internal research test model.

claim_text: The earliest incidents date to April.
quote: The earliest incidents date to April.

claim_text: The models in each of these evaluations ran without the standard safeguards.
quote: The models in each of these evaluations ran without the standard safeguards we deploy when we make the model generally available (that is, they did not have the classifiers and monitoring we usually implement to prevent misuse).

claim_text: The models did have their model-specific safety training.
quote: The models did, however, have their model-specific safety training (that is, they were not the “helpful-only” versions of the models that we sometimes use in testing).

claim_text: The evaluations described here run on dedicated infrastructure.
quote: All the evaluations described here run on dedicated infrastructure, which is separate from and has no access to Anthropic’s sensitive internal systems or customer data.

claim_text: The review began on Thursday, July 23.
quote: We began our transcript review on Thursday, July 23, and stopped all cyber evaluations the same day after identifying transcripts where Claude may have accessed the internet.

claim_text: The three incidents were identified the next day.
quote: We identified all three incidents the next day.

claim_text: The affected organizations were notified on Monday, July 27.
quote: We notified our evaluation partner Irregular and the three affected organizations on Monday, July 27.

claim_text: Two of the organizations had not previously detected the activity.
quote: The two organizations we were able to reach had not previously detected the activity or contacted us, and we are now working with them to remediate.

claim_text: The incidents involved capture-the-flag challenges.
quote: In all three incidents, Claude had been tasked with a capture-the-flag challenge, one of the ways we assess a model’s cyber capabilities.

claim_text: The evaluation prompt specified that the environment was a simulation and had no internet access.
quote: The evaluation prompt specified to Claude that its environment was a simulation and that it had no internet access.

claim_text: Claude compromised the impacted organizations' infrastructure using basic techniques.
quote: Claude compromised the impacted organizations’ infrastructure using basic techniques, such as exploiting weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints.

claim_text: Claude did not exfiltrate itself or deliberately attempt to escape its test environment.
quote: In none of these situations did Claude exfiltrate itself or deliberately attempt to escape its test environment.

claim_text: The incidents involved four runs impacting the same organization.
quote: The incidents involved three different Claude models: Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and an internal research test model.1 The earliest incidents date to April. The models in each of these evaluations ran without the standard safeguards we deploy when we make the model generally available (that is, they did not have the classifiers and monitoring we usually implement to prevent misuse). The models did, however, have their model-specific safety training (that is, they were not the “helpful-only” versions of the models that we sometimes use in testing). All the evaluations described here run on dedicated infrastructure, which is separate from and has no access to Anthropic’s sensitive internal systems or customer data.

claim_text: Incident 1 involved Claude Opus 4.7.
quote: This incident involved Claude Opus 4.7, and was the only case in which the model continued to attack a system after learning it was likely operating in a real environment.

claim_text: Incident 2 involved Claude Mythos 5.
quote: This attack was carried out by Claude Mythos 5.

claim_text: Incident 3 involved an internal research test model.
quote: This attack was carried out by an internal research test model.

claim_text: Claude believed the package registry it was using to be part of the simulation.
quote: Claude believed the package registry it was using to be part of the simulation, but in reality the package was made freely available online for roughly one hour.

claim_text: The package was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.
quote: During that window, the package was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.

claim_text: One of the systems was a scanner belonging to a real security company.
quote: One of these systems was a scanner belonging to a real security company (separate from the fictional company introduced in the scenario) that routinely installs Python packages and scans them for malware.
